title: Standing for justice
hookLine: help your brother, oppressor or oppressed: how do you help an oppressor?
tomorrow: is saying it out loud always the brave thing?

cards: A group chat turns on someone. Screenshots, crying-laughing faces, one person leading it, and that person is your friend. Loyalty says back your friend.

Fairness says the other kid is getting flattened. Then a saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ seems to make it harder: help your brother, whether he is the one doing wrong or the one being wronged. Help the one doing wrong?
That's the odd part. The people listening thought so too, and one of them asked.

teach.h: HOW DO WE HELP THE ONE DOING WRONG?
teach.b: Here's the question, in Sahih al-Bukhari. Messenger of God, we can help him when he's wronged. But how do we help him when he's the one doing wrong?
The answer solves the puzzle. In one report: stop him; that is your help to him.

teach.h: STOP HIM. TAKE HOLD OF HIS HAND.
teach.b: In another: take hold of his hand. Read it twice and loyalty flips over. Helping a friend doesn't mean backing whatever he does.

When he's the one doing harm, the loyal move is to take his hand off the other person. That helps two people at once: the one being hurt, and the one about to carry the wrong. The Qur'an presses it further.

teach.h: EVEN AGAINST YOURSELF OR YOUR KIN.
teach.b: In Pickthall's words: "Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred." Yourself. Your parents.
Your own family. Justice doesn't come with a family discount. And notice what the hadith never says.
It doesn't say drop your friend.
It still calls him your brother, even mid-wrong.
The help changes shape; the bond stays. One to tell someone tonight: in this hadith, stopping a friend who's in the wrong still goes by the name help.

how: Muslims quote this hadith when a friend, relative or their own community is in the wrong: standing with them means stopping the harm, not covering for it.

o: punishing a wrongdoer through a court of law
taking your family's side when they're accused
stopping a wrong, even when your own side does it

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.

s: 'help your brother, oppressor or oppressed' means back your own side, right or wrong
the companions asked how to help an oppressor. the answer: stop him. that's the help.
in the hadith, stopping a friend from wronging someone counts as helping that friend
stop him; that is your help to him.
Qur'an 4:135 asks for justice even against yourself or your parents
against yourselves or your parents or your kindred, in Pickthall's words.

games.q: at work, your closest coworker keeps 'forgetting' to credit the new hire's ideas in meetings. what does today's hadith point you to?
o: talk to your coworker first and stop it; that's helping him too.
say nothing; he's your friend, and loyalty means you back him.
report him to the boss and stop being friends with him for good.
games.why: the Prophet's answer was to stop the one doing wrong, and he called that help. the hadith still calls him your brother: the bond stays.

practice: Hold one hand out, palm forward, the way you'd stop someone gently: not a shove, a pause. Keep it there, breathing slowly, and bring to mind one wrong you've watched happen lately, small or large.
Ask whose hand you might have held, and how kindly. When you're ready, let the hand rest in your lap.

wordCard.voice: Standing for justice: stopping a wrong, even when the one doing it is your own. In the hadith, stopping him is helping him.

orig.note: Arabic: the one doing wrong, an oppressor; the hadith's word for the brother you help by stopping.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: stop the oppressor, and you've helped him as well as the one he hurt. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2444 (also 2443): help your brother, oppressor or oppressed; how do we help an oppressor? take hold of his hands
Sahih al-Bukhari 6952: prevent him from wronging others; that is your help to him

sources.q: Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred
